summary: Describes a way to identify the calling party in the headers of a stored voice mail message. It defines two header fields: one to hold enough information to call back or reply, and one to hold the caller's name.

eli5.summary: It is like a caller ID sticker on a recorded answering-machine message, saying who called and how to call them back.

questions: caller id in voice mail messages
what is the caller-id mail header
how are caller numbers stored in voice mail
subtitle: Two mail headers that keep a caller's number and name with a stored voice mail message.

tldr.problem: When a caller leaves a voice message stored in Internet Mail, the phone network knows the caller's number and name, but there is no good header to keep them in. Squeezing them into the From field is a forced translation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3939 defines two new message headers, Caller-ID for the number (digits only, with an optional NumberingPlan parameter) and Caller-Name for the name, so the information is stored as the phone system presented it.
tldr.outcome: Voice mail systems can show the caller information like a phone display and later work out a reply address. The RFC also lists ways this can go wrong, such as truncated international numbers.

today: RFC 3939 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the VPIM voice message format in RFC 3801.

sections.title: Why Voice Mail Needs Caller Headers
sections.content:
The telephone network usually tells the called party the caller's number and name. When a caller leaves a "Call Answer" message and it is stored in an Internet Mail message store using the VPIM message format (RFC 3801), there is often no RFC 2822 address known for the originator.

The VPIM specification suggests putting the number in the From field, for example From: "416 555 1234" <non-mail-user@host>. Every such option manipulates From. The RFC wants to store the name and number exactly as the phone system presented them, so they can be shown to the recipient and later used to find an Internet address for the caller, if one exists.

RFC 2076 lists a phone header, but it is marked non-standard, has no defined format and has no matching entry for the name. So this RFC proposes two new headers: Caller-ID and Caller-Name.
sections.eli5: A recorded message needs a note saying who called. Stuffing it into the return-address box is clumsy, so this adds two new labeled boxes: one for the number, one for the name.

sections.title: The Caller-ID Header
sections.content:
The Caller-ID header holds enough information for the recipient's voice mail system to call back or reply to the sender. The number is supplied by the telephone system. The number field MUST contain only digits, with no separating characters such as a hyphen, and MUST be representable in ASCII.

For an internal call, such as between two extensions in one company, it is enough to give the extension, based on the company dialing plan. Longer numbers may be supported by the enterprise phone system.

For an external international call, the number must be the full E.164 number: country code, national destination code and subscriber number. Prefixes and symbols such as + MUST NOT be included. E.164 allows up to 15 digits. In North America, 15 digits per T1.625 are suggested, though some providers support only 10 digits.

The other fields available on non-analog systems, such as subaddress and redirecting number, and the meta-data are not meant to be stored in this header.
sections.eli5: The number box holds only digits, like writing a phone number with no dashes or plus signs. Inside a company a short extension is enough, but a far-away call needs the whole long number.

sections.title: Numbering Plan and Date
sections.content:
On analog lines, no numbering plan is known or implied. When it is known, an optional NumberingPlan parameter MAY say what the number means. Only three values are defined:

  • unknown: the default when nothing is known or the parameter is absent.
  • local: the number has meaning only within the domain of the voice mail system that stored the message.
  • e164: the number is as described in E.164.

A value starting with x- may be used for enterprise or service specific dialing plans.

The telephone system may also send the date and time with the number. This MAY be stored in the existing Date header. Whether that header carries the phone system's time or the local system time is a local implementation decision.
sections.eli5: A little label can say what kind of phone number it is, and if nobody knows, it just says unknown. The time of the call can go in the date box that email already has.

sections.title: The Caller-Name Header and Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The Caller-Name header holds the name of the person sending the message. Whether the call is internal or external may be included if available, though this may not be available on international calls. The exact format is typically a service provider option, and names may arrive in several character sets depending on the signaling transport. The RFC lists IRA, Latin Alphabet No. 1, ASCII and T.61.

Where those sets agree, the 7-bit graphical characters are coded the same, so the header uses ASCII. A name that cannot be represented in 7-bit ASCII MAY be stored in its native character set as defined in RFC 2047.

In telephone networks the name MUST NOT exceed 50 characters per T1.641, although providers may limit it to 15 characters for delivery to customer equipment.

Both headers use ABNF (RFC 2234) and the unstructured token from RFC 2822:

"Caller-ID" ":" 1*DIGIT [ "," "NumberingPlan="
  ( "unknown" / "local" / "e164" / ietf-token / x-token ) ] CRLF
"Caller-Name" ":" unstructured CRLF
sections.eli5: The name box is mostly plain letters. If the name has fancy letters that plain text cannot hold, there is a special way to write them down. Names should be short, like a name tag.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples of a stored voice message with the new headers next to the usual To header:

To: +19725551212@vm1.example.com
Caller-ID: 6137684087
Caller-Name: Derrick Dunne

To: 6137637582@example.com
Caller-ID: 6139416900
Caller-Name: Jean Chretien

The headers record the number sent by the analog phone system without alteration or interpretation. If enough meaning is known, it can go in the numbering plan so the number can later be translated into an addressable phone number. Addressable numbers themselves are defined elsewhere, such as in RFC 3191 and RFC 2806.
sections.eli5: The examples show a message with two extra lines: one with the caller's number and one with their name, just like a phone screen.

sections.title: Ways It Can Fail
sections.content:
The RFC describes three failure scenarios.

  • Truncation. A phone system may cut an international number to 10 digits. An Irish number of the form 353 91 73 3307 could become 53 91 73 3307 in North America and be read as 539 917 3307, so a reply goes to the wrong person.
  • Forwarding an extension. If a Call Answer message is forwarded outside the company, an internal extension may be given to an external recipient. That is the wrong number, and it could expose the company's dialing plan.
  • Character options. A system may use coding options that the receiving system lacks, giving the recipient an incorrect Caller Name.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the number gets chopped short and points to a stranger, a company's private extension leaks out, or a name comes out garbled. The RFC warns about these.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registry
sections.content:
Unlisted and restricted numbers are not a concern, because the headers contain what the called party would see, such as Private Name, not the full details exchanged between providers. However, the mechanism does put phone numbers explicitly in mail headers. A recipient may not know they are there unless the client shows them, so the use is meant to be informative, as on a telephone screen.

The RFC creates an IANA registry of Caller-ID numbering plans. Each entry has a token and a short description. The three initial entries are unknown, local and e164. New entries (the ietf-token) can be added only by a standards-track RFC.
sections.eli5: The headers show only what a phone screen would show, so secret numbers stay secret. But since the number now sits in the email, people should know it is there.

items.label: Unknown
items.desc: Semantics unknown; the default when the parameter is absent.

items.label: Local
items.desc: Meaningful only within the domain of the voice mail system that stored the message.

items.label: E.164
items.desc: The number follows the E.164 international numbering plan.

items.label: Private
items.desc: Prefix for enterprise or service specific dialing plans.
